The core problem is semantic, not mathematical: team association and champion residual use the same signed bar language. A negative residual therefore reads as “this dragon hurts Jhin,” although it means “Jhin’s champion-specific term is below the common-only allocation.”

### 1. Receipt + relative-fit plot — recommended

```text
TEAM B · adjusted map-win association  +4.82 pp
All five champions receive the selected dragon buffs

                    Lower fit      Common-only      Higher fit
Jhin       Buff ✓   ●──────────────────│─────────  1.10 pp below common-only
Ambessa    Buff ✓   ──────────────────│──●──────  1.36 pp above common-only
Lee Sin    Buff ✓   ──────●───────────│─────────  1.88 pp below common-only
                      [Champion-informed 3/3]
```

- \(M_0\): rank-0 model with no pair-interaction contribution.
- \(M_F\): full regularized interaction table, using the same training data, regularization policy, clipping, and probability pipeline as every compressed candidate.
- \(M_r\): preregistered nonzero compressed-rank candidate.

All score differences are candidate minus comparator, so negative is better.

### Frozen dual-comparator rule

For each candidate \(r>0\), define:

\[
D^{0}_{r}=\bar L(M_r)-\bar L(M_0)
\]

\[
D^{F}_{r}=\bar L(M_r)-\bar L(M_F).
\]

A compressed candidate is eligible only if both hold:

\[
U(D^{0}_{r}) < 0
\]

\[
U(D^{F}_{r}) \le 0.002\ \text{nats/map}.

The first is superiority to the no-interaction utility comparator. The second is noninferiority to the full regularized interaction representation.

Yes—if “average” means *average by your own betting threshold*, that depends partly on your risk profile, bankroll, and tolerance for variance.

But it is not purely subjective:

- At 3.00 odds and a 36% model probability, the bet has +8% theoretical expected ROI.
- It still loses about 64% of the time, so variance is high.
- Whether your 36% estimate is reliable matters more than personal risk tolerance. A noisy 36% estimate may not justify staking.

For the screenshot, the market’s 1.36 / 3.00 prices include margin. After normalizing the two prices, Rune Eaters’ market probability is roughly 31%, so the displayed +5.2% edge is plausible. I’d describe it as:

> Positive value, but moderate conviction—not necessarily a strong bet.

So “good bet” can be objectively true under the model, while “only average” can still be personally reasonable.

A lot of important debates have the same problem: strong opinions, real consequences, and almost no measurement.

I recently wrote an investigation using a contested decision in a competitive video game as the case study. The subject was gaming. The work was really about data.

What can we observe? What does that observation actually support? Where does the evidence end and the familiar story begin?

Statistics can answer “what tends to happen?” much more easily than “what happened because of this one thing?” That distinction is easy to miss, especially when the answer feels obvious.

If we ignore it, we can turn a chart into confidence without turning it into knowledge.

This is the part of applied AI engineering I enjoy most: taking a question people genuinely care about, defining it precisely enough to test, finding the right data, challenging the easy explanation, and coming back with a result that is useful without pretending it is more certain than it is.
